question: Does process supervision (feedback on each reasoning step) train more reliable reward models than outcome supervision (feedback on the final answer) on challenging math problems?
hypothesis: Process supervision gives more precise feedback and should yield a more reliable reward model than outcome supervision when scaled up.
contributions: Process supervision trains much more reliable reward models than outcome supervision; the PRM solves 78.2% of a representative MATH test subset.
A large reward model can reliably approximate human supervision for smaller reward models and be used for large-scale data collection ablations.
Active learning gives a 2.6x improvement in the data efficiency of process supervision.
Release of PRM800K, the full process supervision dataset.

method.summary: A fixed GPT-4 generator produces step-delimited MATH solutions. Human labelers label each step positive, negative or neutral (PRM800K). PRMs and ORMs, fine-tuned from GPT-4 after a MathMix math pretraining step, are compared by best-of-N selection accuracy. A small-scale regime uses the large PRM as a labelling oracle for ablations.
method.task: reward model training for best-of-N reranking of math chain-of-thought solutions

datasets.name: PRM800K
datasets.size: about 800,000 step-level labels over about 75,000 solutions to 12K problems (filtered); unfiltered 1,085,590 labels over 101,599 solutions
datasets.split: includes data from 4.5K MATH test problems
datasets.source: human step labels on GPT-4 generator solutions; https://github.com/openai/prm800k
datasets.preprocessing: discard quality-control labels and labels where the labeler could not complete the task

datasets.name: MATH (train problems)
datasets.preprocessing: 500 test problems chosen uniformly at random

datasets.name: MathMix
datasets.size: 1.5B tokens (about 1B for small-scale variant without critiques data)
datasets.source: math problems and solutions, math discussion text, synthetic data, critiques grading data
datasets.preprocessing: decontaminated against MATH test with LaTeX stripping and n-gram matching; no guarantee

datasets.name: STEM OOD set
datasets.size: 224 questions (AP Calculus 45, AP Chemistry 60, AP Physics 45, AMC10/12 84)
datasets.source: recent AP Physics, AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AMC10, AMC12 exams

datasets.name: ORM training set (large-scale)
datasets.size: 100 uniform samples per problem from the generator
datasets.preprocessing: no overlap with PRM800K, an order of magnitude larger

models.name: GPT-4 base (large-scale generator, ORM, PRM)
models.architecture: GPT-4, pretrained only for next-token prediction, no RLHF

other.generator_finetune: few-shot generate solutions to MATH train problems, keep correct ones, finetune 1 epoch for newline-delimited steps

models.name: small-scale models
models.init_from: pretrained with roughly 200 times less compute than GPT-4, then MathMix

training.objective: PRM: maximise log-likelihood of a single correctness token (positive/negative/neutral) after each step; ORM: predict solution correctness at every token, final-token score used at test
training.epochs: PRM 2 epochs; ORM 1 epoch; MathMix 2 epochs (about 3B tokens) large, 6 epochs (about 6.6B tokens) small; generator 1 epoch
training.tokens: MathMix about 3B tokens large-scale, about 6.6B small-scale
training.regularisation: ORM: no jointly learned language modeling objective
training.compute: small-scale base models pretrained with roughly 200 times less compute than GPT-4
training.seeds: Fig 4: mean and standard deviation across three seeds

other.lr_note: paper says only that low learning rates were important for stable PRM training; no value given

inference.decoding: uniform sampling from generator; best-of-N reranking by reward model
inference.samples: 1860 solutions per problem generated in total; N up to 1860; for N<=1000 variance over subsamples; OOD set best-of-100; small-scale eval best-of-500
inference.prompting: few-shot to generate generator training data

parameters.prm_score: product of step correctness probabilities, neutral counted positive
parameters.synthetic_label_threshold: step with >20% PRM_large negative probability counted incorrect
parameters.active_learning_mix: 80% most convincing wrong-answer, 20% most convincing remaining; PRM_selector scores 1000 samples per problem

metrics.name: % problems solved (best-of-N)
metrics.definition: pick the solution ranked highest by the reward model, grade by final answer, report fraction correct

eval.protocol: 500-problem MATH test subset; three seeds for small-scale (Fig 4); RM-weighted voting tried with no noticeable gain

results.claim: The large-scale PRM beats the ORM and majority voting at best-of-1860 on the 500-problem MATH subset.
results.setup: GPT-4 fine-tuned PRM (PRM800K) vs ORM trained on 100 uniform samples per problem (different, larger training set); 500 held-out MATH test problems; neutral=positive, product scoring
results.quote: We use our state-of-the-art PRM to solve 78.2% of problems from a representative subset of the MATH test set.
results.note: Fig 3 shows 72.4 (ORM), 78.2 (PRM), 69.6 (majority voting) as bar labels; the training sets are not directly comparable.

results.claim: Active learning is about 2.6x more data efficient than uniform labelling in the small-scale setting.
results.setup: small-scale models supervised by PRM_large (synthetic), best-of-500, 80/20 wrong-answer/other selection by PRM_selector, slope of best-fit lines
results.quote: we estimate that this form of active learning is approximately 2.6x more data efficient than uniform data labelling

results.claim: On out-of-distribution STEM tests the PRM beats the ORM and majority voting in aggregate.
results.setup: large-scale models, 100 test samples per problem, AP Calculus/Chemistry/Physics and AMC10/12
results.note: text says 224 questions; Table 1 row counts sum to 234 (45+60+45+84)

results.claim: Scoring choice matters little: product with neutral=positive is best at best-of-1860.
results.table: Table 4, row neutral = positive, column product

results.claim: In the small-scale comparison process supervision beats both forms of outcome supervision at all data scales.
results.setup: small-scale generator, 1 to 200 solutions per problem, best-of-500, supervision by PRM_large or final-answer check

results.claim: Outcome supervision by PRM_large is more effective than final-answer checking.
results.note: authors treat PRM_large outcome supervision as the more relevant baseline

results.claim: The labelled dataset is mostly incorrect solutions after active learning.
results.table: Table 3, row % end in correct solution, column combined

results.claim: Labelers were screened with 30 quality-control questions and admitted at 75% agreement with gold labels.
results.quote: we only admitted labelers that agreed with our gold labels at least 75% of the time

limits: ORM and PRM training sets at large scale are not directly comparable (PRM set active-learning-biased and an order of magnitude smaller).
The generator is never improved with RL; only reward models are evaluated by best-of-N.
Iterative retraining of PRM_selector was unstable and gave no gain; authors could not diagnose it.
Possible MATH test contamination in pretraining; authors expect relative comparisons to be unaffected.
Which outcome baseline (final-answer vs PRM_large) is appropriate is unclear; the 'negative alignment tax' claim rests on math only.
Optimizer, learning rate, batch size and hardware are not reported.
